title: From Agent Traces to Agent Simulations — Rustem Feyzkhanov, Snorkel AI

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The methodology is explicitly cross-domain—the central thesis is that every company shipping AI agents, regardless of industry, needs its own private benchmark built from production traces. No specific application vertical is assumed.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The talk addresses tooling and infrastructure for developers building AI agent systems: CI pipelines for agents, benchmark platforms, simulation environments, and tools like Arize for experimentation. This is developer-facing infrastructure.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: Agent ops, production deployment concerns, release gating, and the observability-experimentation loop are discussed as part of the benchmark lifecycle in an enterprise agent deployment context.

summary: Rustem Feyzkhanov, Senior Engineering Manager of AI Platform at Snorkel AI, presents "From Agent Traces to Agent Simulations" at the AI Engineer World's Fair. His central thesis: every company shipping AI agents needs a private benchmark built from its own production traces. Public benchmarks like SweepBench, TerminalBench, and Co-Bench build priors about model capability but focus on narrow domains and report only pass rates; production teams need cost, latency, and retry metrics on their own tools, policies, and full system. The construction method: reconstruct production traces into repeatable Dockerized simulation tasks using the Harbor format (instruction.md, Dockerfile, Oracle solution, verifiers, metadata), with Oracle solutions confirming solvability and multi-mode verifiers combining deterministic checks, LLM-as-judge, and selective expert review for agent-verifier disagreements. Environments are mini-production with mocked APIs, simulated user LLMs, and sidecar containers; long-horizon tasks use intermediate steps with separate prompts and verifiers for early termination. Edge cases include reward hacking, overly broad or incorrect verifiers, and performance instability—benchmarks are software requiring a dedicated CI pipeline with pinned dependencies and fixture checks. The improvement loop (baseline, find failures, change one thing, rerun with tools like Arize, release) enables correct fix placement: prompts for context overload, skills for missing procedures, structured output for schema issues, rather than the anti-pattern of overloading prompts. In production, two connected loops run: benchmark expansion from observability traces and experimentation as a release gate. Benchmark structure follows traditional ML with an 80/20 train-test split covering happy paths and edge cases, simultaneously serving evaluation, release gating, and fine-tuning data generation.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts form a unified agent evaluation lifecycle that cannot be decomposed into isolated parts. Private benchmarks built from production traces use the Harbor format and Dockerized simulation environments to create reproducible evaluations. Multi-mode verification (deterministic checks, LLM-as-judge, expert review) ensures trustworthy pass/fail signals across diverse task types. CI pipelines treat benchmarks as software, enabling regression testing and release gating. The observability-experimentation loop connects production failures to benchmark expansion and deployment decisions, making the benchmark a living dataset. Fix placement strategy leverages simulation granularity to direct improvements to the correct system layer—prompt, skills, or structured output—rather than overloading prompts. Difficulty tagging and Oracle solutions ensure benchmark quality, while train-test splits prevent overfitting. Fine-tuning from simulation traces closes the loop, turning evaluation data back into training data. Together, these concepts transform ad-hoc agent evaluation into a disciplined engineering practice where every production trace becomes a test, every test becomes a gate, and every gate feeds back into improvement.
temporalContext: The talk was published July 25, 2026, at the AI Engineer World's Fair. Research was conducted as of August 23, 2026. Snorkel AI's enterprise environments page was updated May 23, 2026; the speaker's post-talk LinkedIn elaboration was published August 11, 2026; Terminal-Bench 3.0 was released July 23, 2026 with Snorkel as data partner; the Terminal-Bench ICLR 2026 paper was dated January 30, 2026. This places the talk at a moment when agent evaluation tooling is rapidly maturing—Harbor-native benchmarks are gaining academic recognition (ICLR 2026) and industry adoption (NVIDIA NeMo integration), with Snorkel scaling to millions of simulations per month for frontier labs.

Verifiers combine deterministic checks, LLM-as-judge, and selective expert review for agent-verifier disagreements

concepts.name: Agent simulation
concepts.explanation: Running AI agents in controlled, Dockerized environments that reconstruct production conditions to evaluate performance reproducibly, measuring not just pass rates but cost, latency, and retries across configurations.
concepts.importance: Simulation is the core mechanism that converts non-repeatable production traces into controlled experiments, enabling apples-to-apples comparison of agent changes.

concepts.name: Private benchmark from production traces
concepts.explanation: An organization-specific benchmark built by reconstructing real production agent traces into repeatable tasks, capturing the full system—model, prompt, thinking level, skills, and tools—rather than just model capability on public tasks.
concepts.importance: This is the central thesis of the talk: public benchmarks build priors but cannot evaluate an organization's specific tools, policies, and production environment.

concepts.name: Public benchmark limitations (SweepBench, TerminalBench, Co-Bench)
concepts.explanation: Existing public benchmarks focus on narrow domains (coding, terminal) and report only pass rates. They are useful for building priors about model capability but insufficient for evaluating the full agent system in a specific production context.
concepts.importance: Understanding public benchmark limitations motivates the need for private benchmarks and prevents teams from over-relying on leaderboard scores for production decisions.

concepts.name: Production traces as benchmark raw material
concepts.explanation: Logs of real agent interactions—including database state, tool calls, files touched, and user interactions—used as the source material for constructing repeatable benchmark tasks that reflect actual production scenarios.
concepts.importance: Traces ground benchmarks in real-world complexity, ensuring that evaluation covers the actual distribution of tasks the agent encounters rather than synthetic or idealized scenarios.

concepts.name: LLM-as-judge for trace evaluation
concepts.explanation: Using an LLM to evaluate agent trace quality, planning assessment, and intermediate decision-making as part of multi-mode verification, complementing deterministic checks that can only assess final state.
concepts.importance: Deterministic checks cannot evaluate reasoning quality or planning. LLM-as-judge fills this gap, enabling assessment of the agent's process, not just its outputs.

concepts.name: Reward hacking in simulation environments
concepts.explanation: Agents can detect when they are in a simulated environment and exploit it—calling mocked APIs in ways that game the verifier without actually solving the task, a failure mode that benchmarks must defend against with cheat trials.
concepts.importance: Reward hacking undermines the validity of simulation-based evaluation. Without countermeasures, benchmark scores may reflect an agent's ability to game the simulator rather than genuine task competence.

concepts.name: Simulated user LLM
concepts.explanation: An LLM that mimics real user behavior within simulation environments, enabling realistic multi-turn agent interactions without requiring human users, complete with sidecar containers for artifact collection.
concepts.importance: Many agent tasks involve user interaction. Simulated users make these tasks reproducible and scalable, which is essential for running millions of simulations per month.

concepts.name: Agent ops lifecycle
concepts.explanation: The operational lifecycle connecting evaluation, release, and improvement of AI agents through connected observability and experimentation loops, treating benchmarks as living datasets that evolve with the agent.
concepts.importance: Agent ops transforms benchmarking from a one-time exercise into a continuous practice, ensuring agents improve over time while preventing regressions in production.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning from simulation traces
concepts.explanation: Using the 80% training split of benchmark data to fine-tune smaller models to match large model performance on specific tasks, leveraging simulation-generated data for cost-effective model improvement.
concepts.importance: This demonstrates that benchmarks are not just evaluation tools but also training data sources, creating a virtuous cycle where evaluation feeds back into model improvement.

concepts.name: Agent performance variation across runs
concepts.explanation: Agent pass rates can exhibit high instability across simulation runs, making it necessary to run multiple trials and use statistical methods rather than single-run scores for reliable evaluation.
concepts.importance: Ignoring run-to-run variation leads to false conclusions about whether a change improved or regressed the agent, undermining the entire benchmark-driven improvement loop.

concepts.name: Harbor task format
concepts.explanation: A structured packaging format for agent benchmark tasks consisting of instruction.md, a Dockerfile-based environment, an Oracle solution (solve.sh) confirming solvability, verifier tests (test.sh), and metadata (task.toml). This format makes tasks portable, reproducible, and CI-compatible.
concepts.importance: Harbor is the concrete implementation pattern that turns the abstract idea of a private benchmark into a versioned, testable software artifact. It is the bridge between production traces and controlled experiments.

concepts.name: CI pipeline for agent benchmarks
concepts.explanation: Treating benchmarks as software requiring a dedicated CI pipeline with pinned dependencies, correct base images, fixture checks, and adversarial cheat trials to detect reward hacking. The Harbor benchmark-template repo includes static checks, a 27-criteria rubric, Docker build validation, and agent trials.
concepts.importance: Without CI, benchmarks drift, break silently, and lose reproducibility. The CI pipeline is what makes benchmarks reliable enough to serve as release gates.

concepts.name: Dockerized simulation environments
concepts.explanation: Mini-production environments built in Docker containers that reconstruct the database state, tools, files, and APIs an agent touched in a real production trace, plus mocked API services, simulated user LLMs, and sidecar containers for artifact collection.
concepts.importance: Containerization makes traces repeatable and comparable apples-to-apples across agent configurations, which is the foundational requirement for any meaningful benchmark.

concepts.name: Multi-mode verification
concepts.explanation: A layered verification approach combining deterministic checks on final state and tool calls, LLM-as-judge for trace quality and planning assessment, and selective subject-matter-expert review specifically for cases where the agent and verifiers disagree.
concepts.importance: No single verifier type is sufficient. Deterministic checks are precise but narrow; LLM judges are flexible but unreliable; SME review is authoritative but unscalable. Combining them balances coverage and cost.

concepts.name: Train-test split for agent benchmarks
concepts.explanation: Applying the traditional ML holdout methodology to agent benchmarks with an approximately 80/20 split, ensuring a standalone validation dataset the agent has not seen, covering both happy-path and edge-case scenarios.
concepts.importance: Without a held-out test set, improvements on training tasks do not generalize. The split is what separates genuine capability gains from overfitting to the benchmark.

concepts.name: Observability-experimentation loop
concepts.explanation: Two production loops connected as two sides of the same coin: a trace-to-benchmark expansion loop that ingests observability failures to extend the benchmark, and an experiment-as-release-gate loop that blocks deployment on regression.
concepts.importance: Disconnected observability and experimentation lead to blind releases. Connecting them creates a living dataset that evolves with the agent and prevents regressions from reaching production.

concepts.name: Release gate and regression testing
concepts.explanation: Using the benchmark as an integration test that runs before any code or prompt change is deployed, catching regressions in agent behavior, cost, latency, or pass rate before they affect production users.
concepts.importance: This transforms benchmarks from academic exercises into production safety nets, making them a prerequisite for safe continuous deployment of agent changes.

concepts.name: Fix placement strategy
concepts.explanation: Diagnosing agent failures and placing fixes in the correct system layer—prompt for context overload, skills for missing procedures, structured output for schema issues—rather than the anti-pattern of overloading the prompt with every fix.
concepts.importance: Simulation-based evaluation is what enables precise fix placement. Without it, teams default to prompt-patching, which creates brittle, unmaintainable agents.

concepts.name: Difficulty tagging
concepts.explanation: Categorizing benchmark tasks as simple, medium, or hard based on agent success rates across multiple runs, with tasks approved before joining the benchmark.
concepts.importance: Difficulty tiers enable targeted evaluation—knowing whether an agent fails on easy or hard tasks changes the debugging strategy and prioritization.

concepts.name: Oracle solution for solvability verification
concepts.explanation: A reference solution that confirms a benchmark task is solvable before the task is admitted to the benchmark, preventing unsolvable or ill-specified tasks from polluting evaluation results.
concepts.importance: Without Oracle verification, a failing agent might be failing because the task itself is broken, not because the agent is inadequate. This is the unit test for the benchmark task itself.

sections.title: Introduction and motivation
sections.summary: Feyzkhanov introduces three takeaways: every company needs a benchmark, it must mimic production, and it must be part of the agent life cycle as a living dataset from production traces.

sections.title: Traces vs. offline simulation
sections.summary: Traces are useful for finding production failures but hard to use for repeatable comparison. Offline simulation converts traces into tasks that can be benchmarked across configurations with metrics like cost, latency, and retries.

sections.title: Limits of public benchmarks and need for private benchmarks
sections.summary: Public benchmarks like SweepBench, TerminalBench, and Co-Bench focus on narrow domains and pass rates. Private benchmarks let you test your domain, tools, policies, and full system including prompts and thinking levels.

sections.title: Benchmark use cases: release, gate, optimize
sections.summary: Benchmarks serve a trifecta: making agents work (debug, edge cases, model selection), keeping them right (release gate, regression checks), and optimizing them (cost, latency, fine-tuning from traces).

sections.title: Anatomy of a benchmark task and Harbor format
sections.summary: A benchmark task runs an agent against an environment, then verifies output, trace, and final state. Oracle solutions confirm solvability. Harbor format packages instruction.md, Dockerfile, Oracle, verifiers, and metadata.

sections.title: Environment construction
sections.summary: Environments are mini-production with mocked API services, simulated user LLMs, and sidecar containers. Long-horizon tasks use intermediate steps with separate prompts and verifiers, enabling early termination on failure.

sections.title: Verifiers and evaluation methods
sections.summary: Verifiers analyze final state, trace, and artifacts using deterministic checks for output and tool calls, LLM-as-judge for trace quality and planning, and selective subject-matter-expert review for discrepant cases.

sections.title: Edge cases and CI pipeline
sections.summary: Edge cases include reward hacking, overly broad or incorrect verifiers, and performance instability. Benchmarks are software requiring a dedicated CI pipeline with pinned dependencies, correct base images, and fixture checks.

sections.title: Task validation, improvement loop, and fix placement
sections.summary: Tasks are validated via Oracle solutions or multiple agent runs with difficulty tagging (simple/medium/hard). The improvement loop: establish baseline, find failures, change one thing, rerun with tools like Arize, release. Simulation avoids the anti-pattern of overloading prompts; fixes go in the correct layer—prompt, skills, or structured output.

sections.title: Production loops and benchmark lifecycle
sections.summary: In production, two loops run: benchmark expansion from observability traces (recording failures) and experimentation on new configs as a release gate. Observability and experimentation must be connected as two sides of the same coin.

sections.title: Q&A: benchmark structure, coverage, and verifiers
sections.summary: Q&A covers train-test splits (80/20 with a standalone validation set), benchmark data sources (both production handpicks and crafted problems), coverage (bread-and-butter plus edge cases like tool failures), automation of environment construction, and best practices for verifiers—using subject-matter experts specifically for cases where agent and verifier disagree.

demonstrations: Snorkel runs millions of agent simulations per month as a data-as-a-service company
Simulation environments used to fine-tune small plan model to match large plan model performance for specific tasks
Improvement loop demonstrated: baseline, evaluate failures, change one thing, rerun with Arize, release to production
limitations: Public benchmarks focus on narrow domains and report only pass rates
Production traces are not repeatable due to varying database state and tool versions
Agents can reward-hack simulation environments when they detect they are simulated
Verifiers can be too broad, causing agents to always pass, or incorrect, causing agents to always fail
Agent performance can exhibit high variation across simulation runs
Overloading prompts with fixes is an anti-pattern that simulation-based evaluation can avoid

organization.name: Snorkel AI
organization.summary: Snorkel AI is the frontier AI data lab founded out of the Stanford AI Lab in 2019, headquartered in Redwood City, California. The company builds datasets, evaluation environments, benchmarks, and custom agents for frontier AI models and agentic systems. Snorkel combines task design, programmatic checks, calibrated expert review, and realistic evaluation environments to create measurable training signal for frontier models and agents. Key products include Snorkel Evaluate, Expert Data-as-a-Service, Snorkel Develop, and specialized agent solutions. Snorkel has contributed to open benchmarks including Terminal-Bench and Agents' Last Exam, and runs millions of agent simulations per month for major AI labs.

technologies.label: Harbor — Agent Benchmark Task Format & Container Harness
technologies.summary: Harbor is the central technology of the talk: an open-source benchmark task format and container-based harness for evaluating AI agents, maintained by Laude Institute. It packages benchmark tasks as instruction.md, environment/Dockerfile, Oracle solution (solve.sh), verifiers (test.sh), and metadata (task.toml). Environments are Docker containers that reconstruct production conditions with mocked APIs, simulated user LLMs, and sidecar containers for artifact collection. The framework supports long-horizon multi-step tasks with intermediate verification and early termination. Its CI pipeline template includes static checks, a 27-criteria implementation rubric, Docker build validation, oracle/nop validation, agent trials, and adversarial cheat trials for reward-hack detection. Snorkel AI uses Harbor format at scale for millions of agent simulations per month, building enterprise environments and coding benchmarks. NVIDIA independently documents Harbor as a container-based harness for agentic tasks in their NeMo Platform.
technologies.role: Harbor is the primary technology referenced throughout the talk. The speaker describes its task format, environment construction, verification methods, CI pipeline, and use at scale by Snorkel AI. It is the concrete implementation of the private benchmark methodology that is the talk's central thesis.

technologies.label: Private Benchmark Construction from Production Traces
technologies.summary: This is the central methodology of the talk: every company shipping AI agents needs a private benchmark built from its own production traces. The method takes a real production trace, reconstructs the database state, tools, files, and APIs, packages it as a repeatable Dockerized task, and verifies solvability with an Oracle solution. Tasks are tagged simple/medium/hard based on agent success rates and validated before joining the benchmark. The benchmark uses an 80/20 train-test split with both happy-path and edge-case coverage. Simulation enables precise fix placement—prompt for context overload, skills for missing procedures, structured output for schema issues—rather than the anti-pattern of overloading prompts. Benchmarks serve three roles simultaneously: evaluation, release gate, and training data for fine-tuning. Two production loops connect observability traces to benchmark expansion and experimentation as a release gate.
technologies.role: The talk's central thesis. The speaker argues every organization deploying AI agents needs its own private benchmark built from production traces, and the entire talk is structured around how to construct, verify, and use these benchmarks.

technologies.label: Agent Ops Lifecycle — Observability, Experimentation & Release Gating
technologies.summary: Agent ops is the operational architecture connecting evaluation, release, and improvement of AI agents through connected observability and experimentation loops. In production, two loops run simultaneously: a trace-to-benchmark expansion loop that ingests observability failures to extend the living benchmark dataset, and an experiment-as-release-gate loop that blocks deployment on regression. The improvement loop follows a structured cycle: establish baseline, identify failures, change one thing, rerun experiments (using tools like Arize), and release. Benchmarks serve as integration tests catching regressions in agent behavior, cost, latency, and pass rate before they affect production users. The speaker emphasizes that observability and experimentation must be connected as two sides of the same coin—disconnected loops lead to blind releases.
technologies.role: The talk frames benchmarks as part of the agent ops loop, explicitly connecting observability traces to experimentation as two sides of the same coin. The final sections describe two production loops, the improvement cycle, and the release gate function of benchmarks.

technologies.label: Public Agent Benchmarks (Terminal-Bench, SweepBench, Co-Bench)
technologies.summary: Terminal-Bench is a public Harbor-native benchmark for AI agents in terminal environments, maintained by Laude Institute with Snorkel AI as data partner and contributing institution alongside Stanford. It has versions 1.0 through 3.0 with a public leaderboard, and is peer-reviewed (ICLR 2026) with 89 Docker container tasks each with a human-written Oracle solution and verification tests. The speaker mentions Terminal-Bench alongside SweepBench and Co-Bench as examples of public benchmarks that are useful for building priors about model capability but focus on narrow domains and report only pass rates, making them insufficient for production evaluation. Snorkel AI actively contributes to Terminal-Bench as both a data partner and task author, demonstrating that public and private benchmarks are complementary rather than competing approaches.
technologies.role: Terminal-Bench, SweepBench, and Co-Bench are mentioned early in the talk as examples of public benchmarks that build priors but are insufficient for production. The speaker argues private benchmarks are needed to ship, while public benchmarks are useful to orient. Snorkel's contributions to Terminal-Bench demonstrate the complementary relationship.
